title: Troubleshooting Common Node.js Problems
learning_outcomes: Describe Module resolution errors and explain how it relates to Troubleshooting Common Node.js Problems.
Demonstrate Port conflicts in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Permission errors.

content.intro: Troubleshooting Common Node.js Problems is part of error handling debugging and diagnostics. This lesson connects Module resolution errors, Port conflicts, Permission errors to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Node.js module systems define how code is loaded, scoped, reused, and exposed to other files. Test importing the public entry point from a separate file, not only running the implementation file directly.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Node.js module systems define how code is loaded, scoped, reused, and exposed to other files. Choose CommonJS or ECMAScript modules explicitly and keep public exports small and documented.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Troubleshooting Common Node.js Problems. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Module resolution errors; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Port conflicts, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing module formats or importing an unsupported internal package path.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Configure package.json and file extensions deliberately, then test the actual public import path.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
